en: The *Upādāyaprajñaptiprakaraṇa* (Treatise on Designation Based on Appropriation), one fascicle.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Dignāga;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by imperial decree.
The treatise states:

In order to preclude the extremes of identity and difference as being non-existent, the Great Teacher merely relies upon conventionally designated phenomena to proclaim the essentials of the Dharma, desiring that sentient beings may enter through skillful means, attend to them according to reality, distance themselves from heterodox tenets, and forever sever the afflictions.
Since all three of these positions are flawed, I shall now provide an exposition.
Within this context, there are briefly three types of conceptual designations regarding causes:
first, the aggregate; second, the continuum; and third, the distinction of states.

Regarding "aggregates" (*samudāya*): this refers to instances where many dharmas are gathered together at one time, and for the sake of worldly convention, they are spoken of as having a single nature, such as "the body" or "a forest.

Regarding "continuity" (*santāna*): this refers to instances where cause and effect proceed without interruption across different times, and are spoken of as having a single nature; for example, the various stages beginning with the *kalala* are called a "person," and the successive transformations of the sprout and so forth are called "grain."

Regarding the distinction of states (*avasthā-prabheda*), this refers to the fact that a single entity possesses multiple natures, which are established at different or non-different times; for example, the state of the arising of form (*rūpa*) is distinct from its impermanent nature, its visibility and resistance, and its status as a basis for action (*karmasādhanatva*), and so forth.
Based on these three meanings, it is taught with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) that there is *pudgala* and the realization of parinirvāṇa.

However, these three meanings are merely provisional designations; they cannot be said to possess a single nature, a distinct nature, or to be entirely non-existent, as each case would entail logical faults.
In this context, let us first examine the expressions "total collection" (*samudāya*) and "collection with no difference in nature" (*abhinnasvabhāva*).

There are only two types of entities; should one grant that these two possess their own intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), or is it intended to negate a difference in their natures? That is to say, is the term "no difference" used because there is no distinction between the collection with existence (*sadbhāvasamudāya*) and the total collection (*samudāyasamudāya*)?
Is it only because there is nothing remaining that it is called "undifferentiated"?
What fault would there be in this?
The verse says:
If there were no distinct nature and no difference in essence, then the collection would be mutually indistinguishable from its parts;
or, if the individual entities within the aggregate were distinct, then this [aggregate] would consequently consist of multiple natures.
The treatise says:

If it were granted that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the hand and so forth is one and no different from that of the body, then because there would be no distinct nature within the body, the hand and other limbs would become indistinguishable from one another; thus, the hand would become the foot, which contradicts worldly convention.

Alternatively, it may be said that those individual parts do not have the body as their intrinsic nature, and that it is only when they are assembled that they are called a "body"; in this case, there would be no whole aggregate with its own substantial entity from which even a small portion could be obtained.
To distinguish it from the preceding meaning, the word "or" (*vā*) is employed.
If, with respect to a distinct entity, it is not the nature of a collective aggregate, then it is a particularity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*).
Given that it possesses a distinct nature, how could it be logically tenable for it to be established as having no distinct intrinsic nature from those [individuals] at the time of aggregation?
This is because a collection does not abandon its own nature;
consequently, it would follow that this [collection] possesses a manifold essence, for a collection has no distinct nature apart from its many components.
Whether considered individually or as a whole, there is no distinct nature, because neither the whole nor the parts abandon their own respective natures.
Whether occurring suddenly or gradually, both result in a manifold nature, because they are not distinct in nature from those various entities.
Thus, the faults of these two positions have been briefly analyzed.
The verse says:
If you say that you merely negate other modes of existence, you incur the fault of [implying] that both [existence and non-existence] do not exist;
if it is a single mode of existence that is negated, then since there is no distinction [between them], the two cases are identical.
The treatise says:

"If it is said that 'if you claim to merely negate other modes of existence, you incur the fault of both [the negation and the object] being non-existent,' then if there were no distinct general aggregate within the collection of existents—such that they were not different from one another—this would mean they are established as non-different by virtue of mutual dependence."
If the meaning of existence and non-existence were not different in one location, it would be the same for a second; how then could you avoid this fault?
Just as there is no "total collection," there is also no "collection."
If it were otherwise, the expression "non-different" would be rendered useless.

If a single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is what is being negated, then even if one were to grant that this is merely the negation of the "named non-different" regarding the real entities with parts (*sāvayava-vastu*) as conceived by others, this too would not be correct, because there is no distinction in the entity itself.

The similarity between the two cases arises from the absence of any statement to the contrary; since it is so in one instance, it is likewise so in the others, because there is no initial statement to the contrary. Therefore, you should not merely negate one case alone.

If you claim that your intention is merely to negate that [existence], then you should simply say "it has no parts" and not say "it is not different," for the latter implies an ontological nature (bhāva) which you do not accept.
If one accepts that their essential nature exists but does not accept that they are distinct, then the statement that they are "not distinct" would be logically consistent.

Furthermore, regarding the point that there is a sense of distinction because they are not non-different, such that the two are similar: just as there is no body other than the hands and so forth because it is a composite whole (*avayavin*), likewise the hands and so forth also depend upon the fingers and so forth to constitute a composite whole; thus, like the body, the hands and so forth are also established as being non-existent.

In this manner, even down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), it depends upon sound and so forth; sound and so forth, in turn, depend upon the sentient being (*sattva*) and so forth; and the sentient being and so forth, again, depend upon joy (*prīti*) and so forth.

Since this [atom] is divided by depending on distinct capacities, and because it shares the nature of having parts (*sāvayavatva*) just like that which possesses parts, what you maintain [as a partless atom] becomes non-existent.
Thus, having briefly established that admitting a distinct nature (anyatva) entails two faults, the verse says:
"A distinct nature is likewise [faulty], because it would exist in part; it would then function separately in each of the constituent parts."
On one hand, there would be infinite fallacies; on the other, it would either not be a unity or be entirely non-existent.
The Commentary states:

"The same applies to being of a different nature. This refers to two fallacies that follow from the preceding discussion: when that [entity] operates upon its own parts, it must either operate upon them individually or operate upon them collectively.
In this context, let us first distinguish the meaning of "partial transformation.
If a part were to transform on one side at locations such as the hand, then that [part] would likewise have another side, just like the hand itself, which would necessarily arise subsequently.
In this way, there would be the fault of infinite regress.
Regarding the phrase "or it is not one," the word "or" is used because otherwise there would be the fault of a different kind of infinite regress.

If one were to say that one side of the parts does not further undergo transformation, then there would be no meaning of a "whole" (avayavin) at all; it would follow that the whole possesses only a single side.

If that were so, one should simply admit that there are only the hands and so forth; why trouble yourself with the partisan insistence that the whole (the "possessor of parts") exists within its own parts?
Regarding the phrase "and entirely non-existent," the word "and" is used because one side would lead to an infinite regress, and furthermore, there would be other faults.
When one side is turned toward a part, that whole [composite] cannot be found at all; for a whole does not possess a "side" in the manner that hands, feet, and so forth do.
If it is argued that when the hands and other parts are separated, there are no distinct constituent parts because the whole (the possessor of parts) is a single entity,
then it follows that [the whole] must exist pervasively at each of those separate locations of the constituent parts.
There are only these two positions, for there is no third conceptual attachment.
The verse says:
"If it were pervasive, it would consist of multiple natures; furthermore, there would be no difference between [the whole] and its parts, such as the hands."
"Or else, because this is not that, it follows that all things would possess the same nature as a single atom.
The treatise says:

If one claims [the whole] is pervasive, then what is accepted as having parts must have parts whose dimensions are identical; since it would be omnipresent in each and every location, it would consequently consist of multiple substantial natures.
Furthermore, there is another distinct meaning, which is why the word "and" (ca) is employed.

This is because [the parts] are omnipresent within a single location; because their existence in separate locations is not admitted; and because the other members do not differ from one another, as there is no distinction in the entity when they are combined in a single place.
In that case, one would have to admit that hands possess feet, which contradicts the principles commonly accepted by the world.
Regarding the phrase "or this is not that," the word "or" is employed because there is yet another alternative view.

To avoid the aforementioned fault, it is argued that while the entity possessing parts undergoes transformation in the feet, it does not undergo transformation with respect to the hands and so forth; thus, there is no fault of [the parts] being in the same location as other limbs. This is like pressing on a goiter until the eyeballs protrude.

If this were the case, all parts would constitute a single substantial entity; consequently, all things would become a single atom (*paramāṇu*). For when those parts arise in relation to their own constituent members, one would find that there remains only the location of a single, real atom.
This single constituent part would then occupy the same atom as the whole (avayavin).
This adherence to the principle of the whole would thus be rendered useless and would contradict one's own tenets.

If it is argued that there exists an atom distinct from form (rūpa) and the other [sensory objects], then the aforementioned fault does not apply; for since that [atom] does not function within the locus of form and so forth, this error does not arise.
This reasoning is also incorrect, for it likewise entails the fault of two-fold attachment.
Therefore, one must admit that this [atom] either possesses distinct spatial parts or lacks spatial parts.
If that were so, what would be the error?
The verse says:
That which possesses spatial dimensions is not an atom (*paramāṇu*).
This is to exclude the notions of identity and difference; otherwise, either many dimensionless [atoms] would not aggregate, or else a multitude would be identical to a single atom.
The treatise says:
Because the atoms as they are thus conceived cannot be established logically, for they possess spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*).
By virtue of these spatial dimensions, they further become divisible into even subtler parts.
Furthermore, because that [self] is negated as being either identical to or different from [its parts], it must therefore be either identical to or different from its own constituent members.
There are only these two possibilities; there is no third alternative to be conceived.

Having already refuted that fault on the grounds that atoms do not possess spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*), since they lack such dimensions, even if they were to aggregate together, they could not be intermingled; furthermore, if one were to concede that they occupy the same location, they would all be identical to a single atom.
However, these atoms cannot aggregate together, because a single atom and the other atoms would mutually obstruct one another;
that is, the substance of all the atoms would become one, as they occupy the same location.
Thus, the faults regarding the identity or difference between the aggregate as a whole and the collection of its constituents have already been explained.
The verse says:
If the continuum were a single entity, it would abandon the state of infancy and gradually proceed through the stages up to childhood.
"One should lose one's own nature, for it is not otherwise; if one says it is not lost, then there would be confusion.
The treatise says:

If one allows for a continuum such that the entity within the continuum possesses no distinct nature, then one must admit that its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is twofold; for this reason, it is called the "continuum-nature," or it merely excludes other [natures].
These two types have already been collectively refuted as a whole; now, regarding the specific distinctions within them, they shall be further analyzed.
When experiencing each distinct stage, does one abandon the preceding stage to experience the subsequent one?
Or should it not be abandoned?
What fault would there be in this?
If one were to abandon the infant, one would lose one's own self upon reaching the stage of childhood.

If you grant that this [self] is non-different from its state as an infant, then at the time of transition, its own essence would necessarily be lost, because there is no distinct nature within this state.
Therefore, your school asserts:
"Regarding all real entities (*dravya*), it is illogical that there should be a distinct dharma arising and a distinct dharma being produced as a transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Nevertheless, they are not non-different, because their states shift and differ in terms of security and peril.
Regarding the statement that they are not different: this is precisely that; thus, for now, we have discussed the fault of [the stages] being displaced and abandoned.

If they were not lost, the characteristics of the phenomena would become confused and intermingled; one would not abandon the stage of infancy to reach the stage of childhood, and because the essential natures of these stages would be intermingled, they would necessarily become indistinguishable.
However, no such thing is observed.
Having already explained the fault regarding non-differentiation,
the verse says:

If they were of different natures, the body would not be stable; to seek stability, one laboriously and falsely constructs it, yet this results in mutual incompatibility as well as arising and ceasing.
If one claims that their substance is distinct and constitutes a real entity, [it is untenable].
The treatise states:

If the continuity of the stream and the substance of that continuity were different, then all the diligent efforts made by those who first fall ill and later seek recovery would be rendered futile, for such a principle would be inconsistent with the nature of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
One has never observed a distinct entity—such as a cow or a horse—that undergoes such a continuity.
If it is argued that an ineffable thing is likewise unobserved, this objection is irrational, for it is precisely what remains to be established.
Because [the self] is free from the two extremes, this phenomenon is observed to exist within the sphere of worldly causes and effects, but not elsewhere.

Furthermore, just as sour wine that is intended to turn sweet would be rendered useless by the efforts of one whose mind is distracted in attempting to cultivate it into a state of tranquility—since their natures are different—so too [would effort be fruitless].
If they were different entities, the principle of arising and ceasing would likewise be inconsistent.
Those things that arise through the continuity of arising and ceasing must operate within the scope of the present factors.
How do the past, future, and present evolve?
Whether it be by way of a single part or in its entirety, both cases have already been refuted as before.
Furthermore, if their natures were distinct, then because the substance of the continuum would be different, there could be no arising or ceasing.
What further fault is there?
If you say they are distinct, then because the characteristics of conditioned phenomena would differ, the continuity you accept would become a substantially real entity.
This is not logical, as will be explained later; the faults regarding whether continuity is identical or different have already been demonstrated.
Furthermore, regarding the distinctions of states, how does this apply to things such as "result-nature" (*phalatva*)?
The verse says:
"In the various states such as result-nature, having apprehended those entities, one applies verbal designations."
If it were different from that, the entity would lack substantiality; if it were not different, the two faults would be as previously demonstrated.
The treatise says:

Having apprehended that entity within its states, such as the nature of being an effect and so forth, one engages in verbal expression; yet [if it were different], that entity would be non-existent apart from those states—namely, when speaking of form and so forth as cause and effect, as identical or different, as self-nature or other-nature, or as having visibility and resistance, and so on.
If one were to say that the entity in question is different from this [subject], then it would follow that it is not a cause, an effect, and so forth.

Furthermore, it would lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because there is no single entity that can be established through verbal designation without depending upon its qualities (*guṇa*) or its own intrinsic nature.
This non-difference in nature entails two faults, as their defects were already demonstrated in the previous summary; they should be reflected upon wherever they may occur.
If one asserts that there is no non-difference in nature regarding existent phenomena—whether in terms of being abandoned or not abandoned—the analysis is likewise as previously explained.

Alternatively, when this [consciousness] evolves within the continuum of the body, it possesses a specific distinction; for example, the taste of beef can serve as a remedy for one suffering from a feverish illness, yet simultaneously act as a cause for its recurrence.
Having already explained the faults regarding the identity or difference of the three types of conventional designations, we shall now analyze the error of those who categorically negate them.
The verse says:
If one does not admit that the body is substantially existent, The teaching of the Dharma without error would be of no benefit.
Furthermore, there would be no persons with wrong views, nor would there be any distinct functional activities.
The treatise says:

For example, regarding the body, one might erroneously describe it as permanent, blissful, self, and pure; conversely, one might correctly teach the Dharma of the four foundations of mindfulness. If the body did not exist, such teachings would be rendered useless.
Furthermore, if one does not admit the existence of a continuum, then the distinction between the antidote and that which is to be remedied would become untenable.
For instance, if one were to grasp another body as being permanent, the teaching of impermanence regarding that very same body as an antidote would be rendered useless.
Furthermore, if there were no distinction of states (avasthā-viśeṣa), the teaching of phenomena such as impermanence would also be useless.

Moreover, those with wrong views who claim that there is no giving, no receiving, and so forth, regarding all meritorious acts consisting of aggregates (saṃghāta), would not actually be holding wrong views;
for all things given, such as food and clothing, are indeed aggregates.
As it is said: "The wind cannot blow, the river does not flow," and so forth;
such statements regarding the absence of continuity are not false views.

However, Buddhism does not admit that those winds and so forth possess real causal efficacy; although they have functions such as blowing, it is not admitted that they can move toward other directions through a continuous succession of arising.
If there were no continuity, such instances of wrong view would not exist at all.

Furthermore, if there were no distinction of states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*), then when one negates both the characteristics of suffering and origination within a single objective field of form (*rūpa-āyatana*), the differentiation of wrong views should cease to exist, because the form itself has no distinction.
Furthermore, there would be no such thing as distinct karmic activities.
Moreover, if one does not admit the existence of a collective aggregate (*samudāya*), then the distinctions in merit regarding monasteries (*vihāra*), stūpas, and so forth, would all be non-existent.
Furthermore, because their mental continuums differ, their merit is likewise distinct.
As the Blessed One told the householder Vīradatta:

"If there were a bhikṣu who, having received and eaten food, entered the concentration of immeasurable mind and dwelt in right mindfulness, then for such [a person], the distinctions in merit would not exist."

If one does not allow for distinctions in states (avasthā-viśeṣa), then because of the absence of such distinctions, the differentiation of functional activity (karmakriyā) would also be non-existent.
For although the underlying entity may not differ, it is commonly accepted that its function is distinct due to differences in its potency (śakti).
Just as when a poison is mixed with other substances it becomes lethal for the sake of treating disease,
so too, those who deny such things as these commit errors.
If there are such manifold faults, why not admit that it exists as a real entity?
This is unreasonable, because it entails those faults. What are they?
The verse says:
Because identity and difference are negated, They are not established through mutual dependence on causes;
Since their own nature is likewise expressible, That which resembles the object arises solely from consciousness.
The Treatise says:

Because form and so forth are substantially existent, and because their nature as being either identical or different when considered in relation to one another can be described, it is impossible to describe their collective aggregates and so forth.
If this is so, how can one body be said to be different from another body? This is because they do not serve as causes for one another.

Generally, when regarding any entity, if the mind abandons that [entity] to grasp this one, it cannot be called a "grasping-cause" (upādāna-hetu) by way of designation, because that [abandoned entity] is not taken as the cause.

However, since the body and so forth exist in mutual dependence, when one is abandoned, the mind does not grasp the other; it is precisely in this sense that "causality of grasping" is a conventional designation.

If form and so forth were abandoned, their collective aggregate would not exist. Therefore, one should know that it is only with respect to the nature of identity or difference within its own specific domain that [the self] is inexpressible, and not with respect to all things.
However, regarding the distinctions of states, the mutual designation of "otherness" (anyatva) and so forth is spoken of as conventional (prajñapti).
If this were the case, then since one does not apprehend [otherness] even in the case of form (rūpa) and other such bases, it would follow that otherness is not substantially existent (dravyasat).
This is logically untenable, because its own essence is expressible, its essential nature and characteristics are distinct and perceivable, and it does not fail to abandon other things.

However, this semblance of an object also arises from consciousness; regarding all objective appearances therein, if they were separate from consciousness, they could not be known. Since their intrinsic nature is likewise a mere designation, there is no fault.
As it is said in a verse:
"Because ghosts, animals, humans, and gods, each according to their respective capacity,
perceive the same location with different minds, it is maintained that the object is not truly existent."
Furthermore, aggregates and the like do not exist as substantial entities, because they lack the nature of being either conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
All phenomena are subsumed under the categories of the conditioned and the unconditioned; these [aggregates], for their part, do not possess the characteristics of the conditioned.
The verse says:

Characteristics are not associated with [the unconditioned] and are not conditioned; if it is said that they exist, this is spoken with intentional meaning (saṃdhāya), for they are also seen to be predicated of the person (pudgala).
If it were unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it should not be subject to destruction.
The treatise says:
If it were conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it should possess the characteristics of being conditioned, such as arising, abiding, and so forth, just like consciousness and other phenomena.
This is not the case; for when a collection of atoms forms a composite whole or a dyad, their characteristics would be infinite, leading to the fallacy of infinity.
Nor can a conventional entity possess such characteristics, because a single thing would then possess infinite characteristics.
However, since at the time when there is the gathering of things that exist as provisional designations (*prajñapti*), arising and ceasing can indeed be discerned;
if one says there is a speaker, then in reality these characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*)—such as this speech and its collective aggregation—do exist.
As a verse says: "All accumulations end in dispersal; All that is lofty must fall;
All unions end in separation; All who have life return to death."

This means that although it is said in the *Samavāya* and other texts that there is the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), and in the *Vihāra* and other texts that there is the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), all such statements are of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*); they do not exist as such characteristics in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).

These characteristics of arising and so forth are known by all people in the world to exist within the conventional; thus, he teaches the Dharma according to those facts, because this accords with the principle of detachment from desire.
Although this is not the ultimate truth, it is spoken thus for the sake of conforming to purity and for the benefit of all sentient beings.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you see a woman who resembles your mother, you should regard her as your mother."

Statements such as these are all merely conventional designations. How can it be known that birth and so forth are taught with intentional meaning (saṃdhāya-bhāṣita) and not in the ultimate sense (paramārtha)?
For birth and so forth are spoken of in relation to the *pudgala*.
For example, it is said that there is a person who appears in the world capable of bringing great benefit to many;
it is further said that all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment;

and it is also said, "I am now old and decrepit and require an attendant," or that "all sentient beings must return to death. Yet, these matters—such as birth and so forth—do not pertain to the person [as a self].
Thus, it has been established that the aggregate and so forth do not possess the nature of being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If that is the case, one must admit that they possess the nature of being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If they were unconditioned, they would not be subject to destruction, because unconditioned phenomena are by definition indestructible.
All composite aggregates and the like should be eternal, just like space and so forth.
It is not possible for composite aggregates and the like to constitute real entities; thus, both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) would be illogical.
Is it not the case that, regarding worldly affairs, there are instances where identity, difference, and so forth cannot be definitively stated? There is such a saying:

It is observed that in the world, people engage in transactions such as buying and selling with respect to things like garments, without ever deliberating upon whether the threads and the cloth are identical or different.
The World-Honored One, wishing to benefit the world, has skillfully proclaimed [the teachings], yet he does not speak of them as being either of one nature or of different natures.
The verse says:
The World-Honored One, wishing to cause the severance of afflictions, Makes them comparable to those things in the world that are subject to thought.
Without speaking of identity or difference, he employs skillful means to teach the Dharma and transform sentient beings.
The commentary states:

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not destroy the world; as it truly exists, they manifest inconceivable matters. According to the diverse dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings—specifically those who are entangled by afflictions and in a state of latent tendencies—they proclaim the essentials of the Dharma in order to sever those various defilements.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do not, like worldly people, engage in useless deliberations.
I declare that I am able to know and see the exhaustion of all outflows; it is not that I do not know or see."
"Up to and including proper mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), and not improper mental attention.
Thus it should be understood that proper mental attention is the primary cause for severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), whereas improper reflection gives rise to manifold sufferings.
One should dispel erroneous thoughts and accord with right mindfulness.
The verse says:
All meaningful accomplishments arise from this foundation; it is easy as a means, yet extremely difficult to encounter.
Physical form and life do not pause for even a moment; the wise should therefore practice swiftly.
*The Treatise on the Provisional Designation of Causes*, one fascicle.
